abstract:
Recently, a high-level
daptomycin (DAP)-resistant Mammaliicoccus sciuri strain (TS92) was identified,
which mediates a 33% decline of DAP when incubated in Mueller-Hinton
(MH) medium. The genetic background of the DAP resistance in TS92
is a newly discovered two-gene operon, named drcAB, whose expression was reported to impair the structural integrity
of DAP, eventually leading to its inactivation. Here, we set out to
elucidate the chemical nature of drcAB -mediated DAP
modification by applying a general unknown comparative screening (GUCS)
approach in high-resolution mass spectrometry. DAP in MH medium was
incubated with Staphylococcus aureu s strain RN4220_P xyl/tet - drcAB, which
carries the drcAB operon under control of an inducible
promoter on a plasmid, and GUCS test and reference samples were obtained
upon and without drcAB expression. A two-step process
catalyzed by DrcAB was discovered, comprising a structural alteration
of DAP. The mass spectrometric data indicate an N-substitution at
the aniline moiety of kynurenine with dehydroalanine and, subsequently,
a cleavage of the ester bond of the DAP core between kynurenine and
threonine by means of water. The structures postulated were confirmed
by comparison of in silico versus measured fragmentation patterns.

Experiments
and Methods
3.1

ATC (Sigma-Aldrich Chemie GmbH, Darmstadt, Germany), anhydrous MH
medium, 70% v/v ethanol, and phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) (all
Carl Roth GmbH + Co. KG, Karlsruhe, Germany), calcium chloride (CaCl
2
), and the LC-MS grade liquids formic acid (FA), acetonitrile
(ACN), methanol (MeOH), and water (Sigma-Aldrich GmbH, Darmstadt,
Germany) were employed. HPLC-Vials and glass inserts were purchased
from Agilent Technologies (Waldbronn, Germany). PALL Acrodisc 32 mm
syringe filters with a 0.2 μm Supor membrane and Eppendorf Protein
LoBind tubes were purchased from VWR International GmbH (Darmstadt,
Germany). The artificial
S. aureus
strain
RN4220_P
xyl/tet
-
drcAB
, carrying the plasmid
encoded
drcAB
genes under control of an ATC-inducible
promoter, was used.

3.2
Instrumentation
and Software
The
incubation of the bacteria was carried out in an SM-30 shaker, covered
by a TH-30 incubator hood (both Edmund Brühler, Bodelshausen,
Germany). The optical density at 600 nm (OD
600
) was determined
with an Ultrospec 3000 pro photometer (Biochrom Ltd., Cambridge, UK).
For sample processing, a Vortex-Genie 2 (Scientific 95 Industries
SI, Bohemia/New York, USA), a Heraeus multifuge X1R centrifuge, and
a Heraeus Fresco 17 centrifuge (both Thermo Scientific, Waltham/Massachusetts,
USA) were used. The chromatographic part of the LC-MS/MS measurements
was performed using an Agilent Infinity II system (Agilent Technologies,
Waldbronn, Germany) equipped with a binary pump G7120A, a thermostated
multisampler G7167B and a thermostated column compartment G7116B.
As stationary phase, a Waters SunFire C18 column (2.1 × 50 mm,
2.5 μm, 100 Å, Waters Corporation, Milford/Massachusetts,
USA) was used. This system was coupled to a Sciex X500R qTOF mass
spectrometer with a Turbo V Ion Source for electrospray ionization.
Automatic calibration of the mass spectrometer was performed using
a Sciex ESI Positive Calibration Solution 5600. The acquisition and
subsequent evaluation of the LC-MS/HRMS data, including the GUCS approach,
were performed using Sciex OS 2.1 software (all Sciex, Concord, Ontario,
Canada).
3.3
Preparation of Standards, Collection, and
Processing of Samples
MH medium was obtained from 21 g of
anhydrous MH medium, which was dissolved in 1 L of deionized water
and sterilized at 118–121 °C and 0.1 MPa overpressure
for 15 min. Stock solutions of DAP in water (5 mg/mL), CaCl
2
in MH medium (50 μg/mL), and ATC in PBS (100 μg/mL)
were prepared separately. An overnight culture of
S.
aureus
RN4220_P
xyl/tet
-
drcAB
in MH medium (37 °C, 200 rpm, 16–18 h) was equally aliquoted
in two parts and subsequently diluted with CaCl
2
in MH
medium to an OD
600
of 0.1. Each aliquot was spiked with
a DAP stock solution to a concentration of 16 μg/mL, while one
aliquot was further spiked with ATC in PBS to a concentration of 100
ng/mL (GUCS test) and one with the same volume of ATC-free PBS (GUCS
reference). After 24 h of incubation at 37 °C and 200 rpm, samples
were collected, sterile filtered, and stored at −80 °C.
For sample processing, 50 μL of both test and reference samples
was separately added into 200 μL of MeOH to precipitate proteins.
These suspensions were immediately vortexed for 10 s and centrifuged
at 4 °C and 14,000
g
for 10 min. 200 μL
of the supernatant was transferred into a HPLC-Vial with glass insert
to be measured.
3.4
Chromatographic and Mass
Spectrometric Conditions
The chromatographic system was operated
under gradient conditions,
employing the mobile phase solvent A consisting of water, ACN, and
FA (100:2:0.1, v/v/v) and mobile phase solvent B consisting of ACN,
water, and FA (100:2:0.1, v/v/v). The gradient started with 10% B
which was held for 2 min, raised to 60% B within 8 min, held for 0.5
min, and in the following 29.5 min, raised to 90% B. Eventually, a
reconditioning step was carried out by decreasing the gradient to
the initial conditions within 1 min, which was held for 4 min. The
injection volume was 10 μL, the flow rate was 0.35 mL/min, and
the temperatures of the autosampler and the column compartment were
8 and 35 °C, respectively.
IDA runs were performed in ESI-positive
polarity ionization mode, applying ion source parameters as follows:
temperature of 300 °C, gas 1 (N
2
) of 50 psi, gas 2
(N
2
) of 50 psi, spray voltage of 5,500 V, curtain gas (N
2
) of 20 psi. The IDA survey scan parameters were set to a
Q1 mass resolution of 1 unit, a collision gas (CAD gas; N
2
) of 7 psi, a declustering potential (DP) spread of 70 ± 10
V, a collision energy (CE) spread of 10 ± 0 V, scanning a mass
range from 800 to 5000
m
/
z
during
an accumulation time of 0.25 s. IDA criteria were set according to
the small-molecule workflow, using a maximum of ten candidate ions
and an intensity threshold of 30 counts per second. The background
was dynamically subtracted. For the IDA-dependent scan, Q1 resolution,
CAD and DP settings were kept, while CE was set to 45 ± 0 V,
scanning a mass range from 150 to 4000
m
/
z
during an accumulation time of 0.1 s.
Targeted HRMS
scans were then conducted based on the results of
the data processing described next, using the
m
/
z
of all unique features selected as precursors. The parameters
from the IDA-dependent scans were adopted, but the mass scan range
was reduced to 100–2000
m
/
z
. The resulting spectra were subsequently used in structural analysis.
3.5
Data Processing and Structural Elucidation
For the GUCS approach employing a non-targeted workflow, data obtained
from measurements of the test and the reference sample were used.
An automated process, comprising a peak finding algorithm with subsequent
comparison of the test and reference samples, revealed all unique
features that were found in both samples. To avoid including peaks
within the noise level, only those features with a minimum area ratio
of ten (test/reference) were selected for further analysis of their
structural composition.
Based on the targeted HRMS scans, sum
and structural formulas were developed by means of the software integrated
formula finder and in silico fragmentation tool, the exact mass (mass
error <5 ppm), the isotopic distribution ratio, chemical restrictions,
and the known fragments of DAP. When all aforementioned conditions
were not in conflict for a proposed molecular structure, it was considered
probable.

body:
Antibiotic-resistant bacteria
are of great concern, especially when they are resistant to multiple
or last resort antibiotics. The 2016 published O’Neill report
warns that antimicrobial resistance (AMR)-related deaths will exceed
those caused by cancer until 2050, unless this trend is slowed decisively.
1
,
2
A crucial step in overcoming AMR is the restricted use of antibiotics.
For evaluation and monitoring the use of antibiotics, the World Health
Organization (WHO) therefore published the access, watch, reserve
(AWaRe) classification for antibiotics whose latest version from 2023
includes 261 antibiotics. The reserve group contains 29 different
drugs or drug combinations, such as the cyclic lipopeptide daptomycin
(DAP), whose application is considered as last resort.
3
Moreover, the detailed elucidation of existing resistance
mechanisms is of great relevance, as it is the basis for both appropriate
surveillance measures and targeted structural modification of the
antibiotic to overcome resistance.
In 2017, the high-level DAP-resistant
Staphylococcus
sciuri
strain TS92, reclassified as
Mammaliicoccus sciuri
(
M. sciuri
) in 2020, was discovered in an AMR study in pig farming.
4
,
5
Initial investigations of the underlying resistance mechanism using
liquid chromatography coupled to tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS)
revealed a significant decline of the DAP concentration after a 24
h incubation of the antibiotic with
M. sciuri
TS92 in Mueller-Hinton (MH) medium when applying subinhibitory DAP
concentrations.
6
The resistance was recently
found to be mediated by the two-gene operon
drcAB
, which was identified by transcriptomic profiling upon DAP pulse-exposure.
The subsequent subcloning of
drcAB
on a plasmid vector
and its heterologous expression in a
Staphylococcus
aureus
(
S. aureus
)
genetic background resulted in high-level DAP resistance in the recombinant
S. aureus
strain RN4220_P
xyl/tet
-
drcAB
. Upon
drcAB
expression, a decrease
of DAP concentration was observed, which was presumably due to DAP
inactivation.
7
However, the molecular fate
of DAP upon incubation with
S. aureus
RN4220_P
xyl/tet
-
drcAB
remains to be
elucidated.
High-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS), e.g.,
by means of a qTOF
instrument, has gained great importance for the qualification of unknown
molecules in complex matrices. By providing high mass resolution and
accuracy (<5 ppm), HRMS acquisition schemes such as the information-dependent
acquisition (IDA) offer the possibility of structural elucidation.
8
−
10
In this study, we aimed at elucidating the molecular fate
of DAP
upon incubation with
S. aureus
RN4220_P
xyl/tet
-
drcAB
, which is carrying the
drcAB
gene cluster being responsible for resistance. We
first deployed a LC-MS/HRMS-based nontargeted, general unknown comparative
screening (GUCS) to mask out matrix-related molecules.
8
,
11
Then, we focused on molecules that have emerged after induction
of the gene expression and aimed to elucidate their structure. This
may facilitate a hypothesis for the resistance mechanism.
1
Results and Discussion
In order to
study the impact of the DAP-inactivating proteins DrcA
and DrcB, DAP was incubated in MH medium with
S. aureus
RN4220_P
xyl/tet
-
drcAB
, which carries
the DAP resistance genes (
drcA
and
drcB
) from
M. sciuri
TS92. These genes
were heterologously expressed under the control of an anhydrotetracycline
(ATC)-inducible promoter. The so-obtained mixture of compounds was
separated by means of a previously developed RP18 gradient LC-MS/MS
method, which served for the measurement of the DAP concentration.
6
The method had to be slightly optimized for separation
and elution of all components and adopted for high-resolution qTOF
mass detection. Considering that DAP (exact mass of 1619.71 Da for
the neutral compound) mainly occurs as [M+2H]
2+
adduct
(
m
/
z
= 810.86) under the selected
MS conditions, the focus was placed on products with a maximum
m
/
z
of 5000.
For the sake of comparison
of the
drcAB
-expressing
strains, the concentration loss of DAP upon incubation with
S. aureus
RN4220_P
xyl/tet
-

was investigated and compared to the previously obtained results
with
M. sciuri
TS92. After 24 h of
incubation, both strains showed a relative decline of DAP of 42% (
Table
1
) and 33%, respectively.
6
It is therefore likely that both the recombinant
S. aureus
strain and the original
M. sciuri
strain are equivalent in this respect,
so as they are in terms of the minimum DAP inhibitory concentration
of 64 μg/mL.

When comparing the
sum formulas of features 1 and 2, it becomes clear that feature 2
formally contains an additional water molecule. Since none of the
fragments in the pattern of feature 2 exhibit a corresponding shift,
this may be explained by a hydrolysis of the lactone moiety of the
core. The fragment pathway of feature 1 (
Figure S3
) implies that the lactone bond may also be cleaved during
the fragmentation process. Nevertheless, ring-closed fragments were
found for feature 1. In contrast, no ring-closed fragment was found
for feature 2 (
Figure S4
), hence indicating
that the lactone moiety experienced a DrcAB-induced hydrolysis. A
corresponding instability was not found in our previous work showing
a constant concentration of DAP over 24 h at 37 °C in MH medium.
6
Since there was also no hydrolysis in the absence
of ATC (reference sample), this reaction cannot be explained by instability
or another enzymatical activity.
The DrcAB-mediated reaction
postulated requires the presence of
the KYN anilino function, which appears to act as a nucleophile. In
addition, another reaction partner is necessary to generate the product
that was found. DAP′s mode of action can be regarded as a kind
of oligomerization, and the site of action is located in phosphatidylglycerol
(PG) and bactoprenyl-coupled lipid-intermediate-rich regions in the
bacterial membrane.
12
Hence, the search
for the second reaction partner is restricted to molecules that can
be found in the bacterial membrane and contain functional groups that
have the potential to act as electrophiles, such as fatty acids or
α-amino acids. According to the fragment shifts found, it must
have a sum formula of C
3
H
5
NO
2
. The
database-supported compound search (PubChem) resulted in nine hits
(
Figure S5
).
13
Due to their close relationship to amino acids, dehydroalanine (DHA)
and its tautomer (2-iminopropanoic acid) represent the most promising
hit. Hence, the DrcAB-mediated amide formation between DHA and DAP
is postulated to inactivate DAP (
Figure
3
). The HRMS data do not distinguish between
both tautomers.
Figure 3
Postulated daptomycin (DAP) inactivation was mediated
in two steps
by DrcAB. (a) First, dehydroalanine (DHA) or its tautomer 2-iminopropanoic
acid (2-IPA) is transferred to the anilino function of the kynurenine
(KYN) moiety of DAP. (b) This reaction is followed by a hydrolytic
cleavage of the lactone bond between KYN and threonine (Thr). Trp:

The α,β-unsaturated carbonyl group
of DHA is a potent
Michael-acceptor and, thus, prone to react with nucleophiles (Michael-donors),
such as thiols, amines, or alcohols.
14
Although
DAP contains some functional groups that may potentially serve as
a Michael-donor, the sum formulas found indicate the amide formation
rather than a corresponding Michael adduct. This observation suggests
an enzyme-driven active transfer of DHA to DAP. The absence of ring-opened
DAP in the reference sample further supports the idea of a two-step
DAP alteration process in which the DHA transfer is followed by ring
hydrolysis. Based on these findings, the existence of transferase
and hydrolase activity can be assumed for DrcAB.
1.4
Discussion on the Plausibility of the Postulated
Structures
With growing molecular weights, the number of
possible sum formulas and their corresponding constitutional isomers
increases. Hence, with regard to structural elucidation using LC-MS/HRMS
approaches, the probable results are becoming increasingly blurred,
particularly for multiple charged ions. Thus, structures proposed
in this process must undergo (several) confirmation stages.
The most reliable confirmation is a targeted approach, in which the
fragment pattern of an authentic reference substance is used for verification.
8
,
15
However, due to the lack of commercial availability or synthesis
strategies, this is not always applicable, as is the case here. This
issue was addressed according to the workflow of Wohlfart et al. by
comparing experimentally and theoretically (in silico fragmentation)
gained MS/HRMS spectra.
16
As the lowest
selectable quadrupole 1 (Q1) mass resolution is 1 unit, isotopes within
this range were able to pass through Q1, resulting in the occurrence
of isotope fragments. This had to be taken into account when evaluating
the fragment spectra. In order to ensure a high reliability for this
type of scoring, fragments with a relative intensity of ≥10%
in each spectrum were considered only. The accordance of these data
was 100% for feature 1 and DAP and 92% for feature 2 (
Tables S1–S3
). A unique molecular structure
was assigned to all but the fragment with the
m
/
z
of 1447.7 of feature 2 (
Figures S2–S4
). Moreover, the measured isotopic distribution ratios of features
1 and 2 did not differ more than 3% from their respective theoretical
value (
Figure S6
). Hence, the assumptions
made previously and thus the structures proposed were confirmed.
The occurrence of the DHA moiety as an artifact, which emerges
from amino acids, such as alanine, cysteine, or serine during the
MS-ionization process, is theoretically possible. However, this scenario
is unlikely to occur since ESI is a soft ionization technique.
17
Moreover, no similar phenomena were observed
for DAP, and the respective features occur only in the samples in
which the
drcAB
gene cluster was expressed. Nevertheless,
it is plausible that DHA originates from cysteine or serine, as these
are typical precursors in the biosynthesis of DHA.
18
Recent structure–activity relationship models
of DAP attribute
KYN a crucial role in the interaction with the lipid bilayer, in the
binding of calcium, and therefore in the antibacterial activity. In
particular, Taylor and Palmer demonstrated a 47-fold loss of activity
after replacing KYN with tyrosine, whereas Chow et al. demonstrated
an increase in activity after KYN
N
-methylation.
19
−
22
KYN
N
-methylated DAP (kynomycin) has been shown
to possess a 2–4-fold higher antibacterial activity than DAP
and to eradicate certain DAP-resistant strains.
22
The improved antibacterial profile of kynomycin could now
likely be explained by a reduced accessibility of transferases to
N
-methylated KYN. Hence, KYN N-substitution appears to be
a promising bacterial mechanism to confer increased DAP insusceptibility
in general. In the second stage of the
drcAB
-induced
DAP inactivation, a hydrolysis of the lactone bond along with linearization
of DAP-DHA was observed. This is remarkable considering that this
linearization would be sufficient for DAP inactivation, as demonstrated
by D’Costa et al.
23
However, from
the bacterial perspective, the combination of these two mechanisms
will certainly ensure efficacy to combat DAP.
Apart from that,
the question of the origin of DHA or its derivatives
arises. Grein et al. postulated the interruption and delocalization
of the cell wall biosynthesis machinery (transpeptidase and transglycosylase)
as the main mode of action of DAP. They were able to demonstrate the
formation of a tripartite complex of Ca
2+
-DAP with PG and
bactoprenyl-coupled lipid intermediates (lipids I and II) within the
membrane.
12
The transpeptidase releases
d
-alanine, a DHA derivative, upon the cross-linking of the peptidoglycan
units.
24
,
25
Along with that, DrcAB is known to be a
membrane-associated enzyme complex which is supposed to span the entire
membrane.
7
Thus, all of the enzymes and
putative substrates involved are located close to each other. Also,
the general possibility of modifications by transfer of amino acids,
such as alanine in Gram-positive bacteria, has already been described,
making the mechanism a plausible scenario.
26
2
Conclusions
The generation of
S. aureus
RN4220_P
xyl/tet
-
drcAB
can be considered a decisive
tool as it enabled GUCS by providing test and reference samples. IDA
data gained from LC-MS/HRMS measurements revealed the presence of
two molecules, features 1 and 2, that emerged upon the heterologous
expression of
drcAB
. Their structural elucidation
was performed under consideration of the corresponding mass spectrometric
data. With the knowledge of the DAP fragmentation pattern, features
1 and 2 were found to be DAP-derivatives that were generated by a
DrcAB-mediated two-step process. This mechanism comprises N-substitution
of the arylamine moiety of KYN with C
3
H
4
NO and
a subsequent hydrolysis of the lactone moiety. Hence, DrcAB was shown
to possess both transferase and hydrolase activity. The combined data
led us to the hypothesis that DHA is transferred to DAP, resulting
in DAP-DHA and along with this to a DAP inactivation. Bacteria have
evolved a broad variety of transferases to add molecules or groups
to potentially hazardous compounds, including antibiotics. A well-known
and prime example is the modification (and inactivation) of aminoglycosides
by acetylation, phosphorylation, or nucleotidylation. For lipopeptides,
however, resistance through modifying enzymes has not been observed
so far. By attributing transferase and hydrolase activity to DrcAB,
we expand the antibiotic modifying resistance mechanisms to DAP and
describe (to the best of our knowledge) for the first time the transfer
of DHA to a KYN moiety in nature.

3.4
Chromatographic and Mass
Spectrometric Conditions
The chromatographic system was operated
under gradient conditions,
employing the mobile phase solvent A consisting of water, ACN, and
FA (100:2:0.1, v/v/v) and mobile phase solvent B consisting of ACN,
water, and FA (100:2:0.1, v/v/v). The gradient started with 10% B
which was held for 2 min, raised to 60% B within 8 min, held for 0.5
min, and in the following 29.5 min, raised to 90% B. Eventually, a
reconditioning step was carried out by decreasing the gradient to
the initial conditions within 1 min, which was held for 4 min. The
injection volume was 10 μL, the flow rate was 0.35 mL/min, and
the temperatures of the autosampler and the column compartment were
8 and 35 °C, respectively.

3.5
Data Processing and Structural Elucidation
For the GUCS approach employing a non-targeted workflow, data obtained
from measurements of the test and the reference sample were used.
An automated process, comprising a peak finding algorithm with subsequent
comparison of the test and reference samples, revealed all unique
features that were found in both samples. To avoid including peaks
within the noise level, only those features with a minimum area ratio
of ten (test/reference) were selected for further analysis of their
structural composition.
Based on the targeted HRMS scans, sum
and structural formulas were developed by means of the software integrated
formula finder and in silico fragmentation tool, the exact mass (mass
error <5 ppm), the isotopic distribution ratio, chemical restrictions,
and the known fragments of DAP. When all aforementioned conditions
were not in conflict for a proposed molecular structure, it was considered
probable.
